notes: Ruling slot 0 = Thieu's National Social Democratic Front; coalition slot 13 = the Tran Thien Khiem cabinet. Religious slots map Buddhist/sect politics: Quoc Tu moderates 8, An Quang UBCV 9, Cao Dai Holy See 10, militant Hoa Hao 11, Hoa Hao Dan Xa party 12. Communists: PRP 4, NLF 5, PRG 19 (southern-autonomist face), Alliance 18. Ky faction in 7, Diemist Can Lao remnants in 6.

0.name: Mat tran Quoc gia Dan chu Xa hoi
0.native_full: Mat tran Quoc gia Dan chu Xa hoi
0.text:
The National Social Democratic Front was launched by President Nguyen Van Thieu in 1969 as the political base of his government, a federation of Catholic, Hoa Hao, Dai Viet, nationalist and labour groups pledged to support the presidency. Thieu, a general who won the 1967 election, leads it with the backing of Prime Minister Tran Thien Khiem and the province chiefs.

The front stands for a strong presidency, anti-communism, alliance with the United States and Vietnamization of the war, promising land reform and social welfare to compete with the NLF. Its weakness is that its members follow their own leaders more than Thieu; its strength is the presidency, the administration and American aid.

1.name: Luc luong Dai Doan ket
1.text:
The Greater Solidarity Force is the political organization of militant Catholics, built largely on the refugees who fled the North in 1954–55 and settled in parishes around Saigon, Bien Hoa and the coast. Led by Nguyen Gia Hien, it has joined Thieu's National Social Democratic Front while keeping its own network of priests, parish militias and deputies.

It stands for uncompromising anti-communism, the defence of the Church, a strong state and close alliance with America, and it remembers Diem's fall with bitterness toward the Buddhist activists. Its leverage lies in disciplined parish votes, Catholic officers in the army and refugee villages that will fight rather than live under communism again.

2.name: Phong trao Quoc gia Cap tien
2.native_full: Phong trao Quoc gia Cap tien
2.text:
The Progressive Nationalist Movement was founded in 1969 by Professor Nguyen Ngoc Huy, the Dai Viet theorist, and Nguyen Van Bong, rector of the National Institute of Administration, as a modern opposition party within the constitutional system. It draws on Huy's New Dai Viet group and on civil servants, lecturers and lawyers in Saigon and the Mekong Delta.

The movement calls for a loyal opposition, the rule of law, decentralization, land reform and a negotiated peace from strength, rejecting both communism and military rule. It is pro-American in outlook but critical of Thieu's personal power, and its leverage lies in its ideas, its educated cadres and its standing with Western embassies.

3.name: Tong Lien doan Lao cong Viet Nam
3.native_full: Tong Lien doan Lao cong Viet Nam
3.text:
The Vietnamese Confederation of Labor is South Vietnam's largest trade union federation, founded in 1952 and led by Tran Quoc Buu, who claims several hundred thousand members among dockers, plantation workers, tenant farmers and fishermen. Backed by the AFL-CIO and the Christian labour internationals, it survived Diem's hostility and remains an independent force.

The CVT demands land for tenants, wage protection against wartime inflation, social insurance and a voice for workers in government, and Buu is building a farmer-worker party around it. It is firmly anti-communist and pro-American, and its leverage lies in its power to halt the port of Saigon and the rubber plantations.

4.name: Dang Nhan dan Cach mang Viet Nam
4.native_full: Dang Nhan dan Cach mang Viet Nam
4.text:
The People's Revolutionary Party was proclaimed in January 1962 as the Marxist-Leninist party of the South, in reality the southern branch of the Vietnam Workers' Party in Hanoi. It directs the insurgency through the Central Office for South Vietnam, headed by Pham Hung, and its cadres hold the real command posts inside the NLF, the PRG and the Liberation Armed Forces.

The party aims at the overthrow of the Saigon government, the expulsion of American forces and reunification under socialism, following Le Duan's strategy of combined military and political struggle. Battered by the losses of 1968, it still commands tens of thousands of cadres, and its leverage lies in discipline, Northern support and the village underground.

5.name: Mat tran Dan toc Giai phong mien Nam Viet Nam
5.native_full: Mat tran Dan toc Giai phong mien Nam Viet Nam
5.text:
The National Front for the Liberation of South Vietnam, founded in December 1960, is the broad insurgent front its enemies call the Viet Cong. Chaired by the Saigon lawyer Nguyen Huu Tho, it groups peasant, women's, youth and religious associations and fields the Liberation Armed Forces; since June 1969 it has formed the Provisional Revolutionary Government with its allies.

The front promises land to the tiller, an end to foreign occupation, a neutral South and eventual reunification, and wages guerrilla war across the countryside. Although many of its southern cadres fell in 1968, it still controls or contests much of the delta and the central coast, and its leverage lies in rural support and armed struggle.

6.name: Can Lao Nhan vi Cach mang Dang
6.native_full: Can Lao Nhan vi Cach mang Dang
6.text:
The Personalist Labor Revolutionary Party was the secret ruling party of President Ngo Dinh Diem, organized by his brother Ngo Dinh Nhu to control the army, the police and the civil service. Dissolved after the coup of November 1963 that killed both brothers, it survives on 1 January 1970 as an underground network of former officials, Catholic officers and Central Vietnamese loyalists who revere Diem's memory.

Its adherents preach Nhu's personalism, a disciplined one-party state and Vietnamese sovereignty against both communism and American interference; they blame Washington for Diem's murder and distrust the generals who rule. Their leverage lies in old files, quiet loyalties in the bureaucracy and the bitterness of those purged after 1963.

7.name: Phe Ky
7.text:
Phe Ky is the clique of Vice President Nguyen Cao Ky, the flamboyant air marshal who led the government in 1965–67 before Thieu outmanoeuvred him. Its core lies in the Air Force, among Northern-born officers and in the remains of the police network that Ky's ally General Nguyen Ngoc Loan ran until 1968.

Ky speaks for a harder, more Vietnamese nationalism: strong-man rule, total mobilization against the communists, contempt for corrupt politicians and growing resentment of American tutelage and secret peace talks. The faction is at odds with Thieu, and its leverage lies in aircraft, loyal colonels and Ky's popularity with young officers.

8.name: Phat giao Quoc Tu
8.text:
Phat giao Quoc Tu is the moderate Buddhist faction centred on the Vietnam Quoc Tu pagoda in Saigon and led by the venerable Thich Tam Chau, a Northern-born monk who broke with the militant An Quang leadership in 1966–67. The government recognized his faction's charter in 1967, and it enjoys state favour, broadcasting time and funds.

It wants a public voice for Buddhism, social work, schools and chaplaincies for Buddhist soldiers, but avoids street protest and accepts the anti-communist alliance with America. Its support comes from Northern refugee Buddhists and Saigon's middle class, and its leverage lies in its access to the government.

9.name: Giao hoi Phat giao Viet Nam Thong nhat
9.native_full: Giao hoi Phat giao Viet Nam Thong nhat
9.text:
The Unified Buddhist Church of Vietnam, headquartered at the An Quang pagoda in Saigon, is the activist Buddhist leadership that helped bring down Diem in 1963 and led the Struggle Movement of 1966 in Hue and Da Nang. Its guiding figure is the venerable Thich Tri Quang, and its moral authority rests on the Supreme Patriarch Thich Tinh Khiet.

The An Quang monks demand civilian rule, an end to military dictatorship, a negotiated peace and a South free of foreign troops, and regard Thieu as heir to Diem's Catholic favouritism. They command student and youth associations and the pagodas of Central Vietnam, and their leverage lies in mass protest and the votes of the Buddhist majority.

10.name: Toa thanh Tay Ninh
10.english: Cao Dai Holy See of Tay Ninh
10.text:
The Holy See of Tay Ninh is the central church of Caodaism, the syncretic faith founded in 1926 that venerates the Buddha, Confucius, Jesus and Victor Hugo among its saints and counts over a million followers in the South. Its great leader Pham Cong Tac died in exile in 1959; on 1 January 1970 the See is governed by its councils of dignitaries under watchful government eyes.

Once a state within the state with its own army, Cao Dai now seeks autonomy for its province, protection for its temples and a share of power in Saigon, with a strong current favouring a neutral peace. Its leverage lies in disciplined congregations around Tay Ninh and its votes in the Assembly.

11.name: Nghia quan Ba Cut
11.text:
Nghia quan Ba Cut is the name taken by militant Hoa Hao believers who keep faith with Ba Cut, the sect general executed by Diem in 1956 after refusing to merge his army into the national forces. Scattered through An Giang and Chau Doc, they keep weapons, venerate the vanished prophet Huynh Phu So and reject the compromises of Hoa Hao politicians in Saigon.

They await the prophet's return and a righteous Hoa Hao order in the western delta, hate the communists who killed So in 1947 and distrust Saigon and the Americans alike. They are few but armed, and their leverage lies in local militias, religious fervour and delta villages that answer to no outsider.

12.name: Viet Nam Dan chu Xa hoi Dang
12.native_full: Viet Nam Dan chu Xa hoi Dang
12.text:
The Vietnam Social Democratic Party, known as Dan Xa, is the political arm of the Hoa Hao Buddhist sect, founded in 1946 by the prophet Huynh Phu So shortly before his murder by the Viet Minh. Divided into rival factions, one of which has joined Thieu's National Social Democratic Front, it dominates local politics in An Giang and the western Mekong Delta.

The party seeks a moral politics drawn from Hoa Hao teaching: peasant welfare, simple living, autonomy for the sect's provinces and fierce anti-communism. It accepts the American alliance for security but defends Hoa Hao interests above all, and its leverage lies in a million faithful and regional forces that keep the communists out of its heartland.

13.name: Chinh phu Viet Nam Cong hoa
13.english: Government of the Republic of Vietnam
13.native_full: Chinh phu Viet Nam Cong hoa
13.text:
The Government of the Republic of Vietnam is the cabinet led since September 1969 by Prime Minister Tran Thien Khiem, a general and close ally of Thieu, which replaced the civilian cabinet of Tran Van Huong. It combines generals, career administrators and Western-trained technocrats who run the ministries, the province chiefs and the national police.

The cabinet carries out pacification, prepares the Land to the Tiller reform and manages American-funded development. It is loyal to the president and the American alliance but jealous of its own prerogatives, and its leverage lies in administration, police files and the distribution of rice, fuel and aid.

14.name: Viet Nam Quoc dan Dang
14.text:
The Vietnamese Nationalist Party, founded in 1927 on the model of the Kuomintang, survives in the South as a cluster of rival factions after decades of repression by the French, the Viet Minh and Diem. Its strongest base lies in the central provinces of Quang Nam and Quang Tin, where its cadres hold local office, provincial seats and command of village militias.

The party upholds Sun Yat-sen's three principles, a nationalist republic and an anti-communism born of the Viet Minh's killings of its members in 1946. It is regional, clannish and suspicious of Saigon's generals, and its leverage lies in central Vietnamese villages, the prestige of its martyrs and its seats in the National Assembly.

15.name: Hoa thuong Cho Lon
15.text:
Hoa thuong Cho Lon are the Chinese merchant houses of Cholon, Saigon's twin city, organized in their Cantonese, Teochew, Hokkien, Hakka and Hainanese congregations. They control most of the South's rice trade, milling, money-lending and import business, and their fortunes have swollen with American spending and wartime shortages.

Politically discreet, they buy protection from generals, province chiefs and police, and are accused of profiteering, speculation and even dealing with the communists. They favour any regime that keeps the ports open and the piastre stable, and their leverage is money: no government can feed Saigon without them.

16.name: Kinh te Tu do
16.text:
Kinh te Tu do is the group of young Western-trained economists around Pham Kim Ngoc, Minister of Economy in the Khiem cabinet, together with bankers and Saigon businessmen who want to free the war economy from controls. They are preparing devaluation of the piastre, an end to import licensing and incentives for private investment and exports.

The group argues that only market reforms can curb inflation, reduce dependence on American aid and give the South an economy able to survive the departure of US troops. It is pro-American, technocratic and unpopular with merchants living off licences, and its leverage lies in the ministries, the National Bank and the trust of USAID.

17.name: Dong Xanh
17.text:
Dong Xanh is a loose circle of agronomists, Buddhist social workers and students in Saigon and Can Tho alarmed by the war's damage to the land: the defoliation of forests and mangroves by American herbicides, the crater fields left by bombing and the ruin of orchards and rice paddies in the delta.

They call for an end to herbicide spraying, the replanting of forests and mangroves, protection of the Mekong's fisheries and help for farmers whose crops have been poisoned. The circle avoids open alignment with either camp, and its leverage is moral: reports, testimony and photographs that embarrass Saigon and Washington before the world press.

18.name: Lien minh cac Luc luong Dan toc, Dan chu va Hoa binh
18.english: Alliance of National, Democratic and Peace Forces
18.native_full: Lien minh cac Luc luong Dan toc, Dan chu va Hoa binh Viet Nam
18.text:
The Alliance of National, Democratic and Peace Forces was formed in April 1968, after the Tet Offensive, by Saigon and Hue intellectuals who left the cities to join the revolution. Its chairman is the lawyer Trinh Dinh Thao, and since June 1969 it has been the NLF's partner in the Provisional Revolutionary Government.

The Alliance speaks for a neutral, democratic South Vietnam, social reform and a coalition government after American withdrawal, appealing to urban professionals, students and Buddhists who will not join the communists. Its leverage lies in respectability abroad and in giving the revolution a face the urban middle class can accept.
18.wiki: Alliance of National, Democratic, and Peace Forces

19.name: Chinh phu Cach mang Lam thoi Cong hoa mien Nam Viet Nam
19.native_full: Chinh phu Cach mang Lam thoi Cong hoa mien Nam Viet Nam
19.text:
The Provisional Revolutionary Government was proclaimed in June 1969 by the NLF and the Alliance as a rival state to Saigon, with the architect Huynh Tan Phat as president and Nguyen Thi Binh as foreign minister and delegate to the Paris peace talks. It is recognized by the communist states and a growing list of non-aligned governments.

The PRG claims to speak for a separate, neutral South that would reunify with the North only gradually, and many of its southern members cherish that autonomy. Its leverage is diplomatic: a seat in Paris, recognition across the Third World and a claim to legitimacy that the American war seeks to deny it.
19.wiki: Provisional Revolutionary Government of the Republic of South Vietnam

20.name: Dang Dai Viet Cach mang
20.text:
The Revolutionary Dai Viet Party was founded in the mid-1960s by Ha Thuc Ky, a veteran of the Dai Viet Nationalist Party, as a populist anti-communist party rooted in Hue and the central provinces. Ky stood for president in 1967, and the party now holds seats in the National Assembly and a place in Thieu's front.

It calls for total victory over communism, mass mobilization of the people, social justice for the poor and an end to corruption, and attacks Buddhist neutralists as communist dupes. It backs the American war effort but resents foreign control, and its leverage lies in disciplined cadres and Central Vietnamese militias.

21.name: Dai Viet Quoc dan Dang
21.text:
The Dai Viet Nationalist Party was founded in 1939 by Truong Tu Anh, whose doctrine of 'national survivalism' borrowed from European fascism and Japanese ultranationalism. After his disappearance in 1946 it split into Northern, Central and Southern branches; on 1 January 1970 its veterans sit in the army, the ministries and the Assembly while its splinters quarrel over the leadership.

The core faithful still preach an elitist, militarized nationalism: a disciplined vanguard, a unified Vietnam purged of communism and a state above parties and religions. They cooperate with the Americans out of necessity, and their leverage lies in officers and officials recruited over three decades who answer to the party cell before the government.

22.name: Quan luc Viet Nam Cong hoa
22.native_full: Quan luc Viet Nam Cong hoa
22.text:
The Republic of Vietnam Armed Forces number about a million men in regular and territorial units, expanding fast under President Nixon's Vietnamization policy. Commanded through the Joint General Staff of General Cao Van Vien, they are the true power in the South: generals have ruled since 1963, and the four corps commanders govern their regions almost as warlords.

The officer corps is anti-communist and dependent on American arms, pay and air power, but divided by regional, religious and personal loyalties to Thieu, Ky and Duong Van Minh. Its leverage is decisive: no government can stand without its consent, and any general with troops near Saigon is a potential president.

23.name: Nha Nguyen
23.text:
The Nguyen dynasty ruled Vietnam from 1802 until Emperor Bao Dai abdicated to the Viet Minh in 1945; restored as head of the State of Vietnam, he was deposed by Diem's rigged referendum in 1955. On 1 January 1970 Bao Dai lives quietly in France, and his heir, Crown Prince Bao Long, also lives abroad.

Monarchists in Hue and among older Southern notables see the throne as a symbol above the warring generals and parties, able to reconcile North and South in a neutral, traditional Vietnam. They have no organization of weight, but the dynasty's name still carries prestige in the old imperial city and among those exhausted by war.
